statement: SPRAT is a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies.
evidence_summary: [initial_requirement:INITIAL_REQUIREMENTS] Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.

statement: SPRAT is intended for use during requirements and analysis work before design is finalized, and it remains useful during review, change impact analysis, and compliance checks.
evidence_summary:
[interview_turn:T018] We’d expect it to be used very early, during requirements and analysis work, before design is finalized. That’s when people are identifying goals, mapping policies, and shaping the initial requirements set.
Later on, it would still be useful during review, change impact analysis, and compliance checks, but probably less for day-to-day implementation work. If a project is closed or fully handed over, usage would likely taper off except for audits or lessons learned.

statement: The system shall support administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests with role-appropriate access.
evidence_summary:
[initial_requirement:INITIAL_REQUIREMENTS] Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.; [interview_turn:T020] For day one, the core scenarios are capturing goals, policies, scenarios, and requirements; linking them together so the rationale is traceable; and letting people compare two analyses side by side. We also need the basic role-based access so administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests can each do the right level of work.
What can wait are the nicer workflow features, automation, and deeper reporting. The first release has to prove that teams can organize the analysis, review it, and trust the traceability without needing extra bells and whistles.; [interview_turn:T058] Project managers should be able to review, comment, compare analyses, and check traceability, but they shouldn’t have unrestricted editing unless that’s part of their role on the project. Guests should be read-only, so they can view approved materials and maybe compare published analyses if allowed, but not change anything or see restricted details.
I’d also block guests from viewing sensitive notes, draft legal-compliance information, and any unapproved trace links unless the project owner explicitly grants access.; [interview_turn:T068] Yes, role should absolutely affect it. Analysts and project managers can usually generate the full internal exports, while guests should only be able to access approved, redacted versions if they get export access at all. Administrators would have the broadest access, especially for audit or compliance purposes.
The level of detail should drop automatically for lower roles, so things like draft comments, sensitive source links, and personal data are excluded. In some cases, the role should block export entirely if the user is trying to pull something classified above their clearance or outside their project scope.

statement: The system shall allow users to link requirements, goals, policies, scenarios, and derived analyses so that the rationale is traceable.
evidence_summary:
[interview_turn:T002] The main outcome is that analysts can produce a clear, traceable set of requirements that shows how web-system features line up with security and privacy obligations. In practice, that means we can point from a requirement or goal back to the source policy or legal rule, and we can see that nothing important was missed.
It would be meeting expectations if different people can independently build analyses and then compare them without losing the reasoning behind decisions. Another practical sign is that the workbench helps us catch gaps or conflicts early, before the requirements move forward into implementation or review.; [interview_turn:T008] We need the workbench to show which requirement supports which goal, and which policy or legal source justified that goal or requirement. In many cases one requirement will map to several goals, and one policy will drive many requirements, so the tool has to represent those many-to-many relationships cleanly.
It’s also important to capture overlaps and dependencies, because analysts often reuse the same policy interpretation across different parts of the analysis. If a requirement was derived through another requirement or a scenario, that connection should be visible too so someone reviewing it can understand the reasoning, not just the final statement.; [interview_turn:T020] For day one, the core scenarios are capturing goals, policies, scenarios, and requirements; linking them together so the rationale is traceable; and letting people compare two analyses side by side. statement: The system shall support a gradual migration of existing analysis work into SPRAT.
evidence_summary:
[interview_turn:T030] The main scenario is that teams already have analysis work in documents, spreadsheets, or other tools, and they need a practical way to bring the important parts into SPRAT without starting from scratch. The key outcome is preserving the traceability and context of what they already know, so the migrated work is still trustworthy and reviewable.
For scope, I’d focus first on getting the core content and links across cleanly, even if some formatting or historical clutter is left behind. The transition should support a gradual move rather than forcing a big-bang cutover.; [interview_turn:T070] We’d migrate first the active projects, the authoritative source documents, and anything needed to maintain traceability for current work. Older drafts, duplicates, and reference material that isn’t being used right now can stay in the old tools for a while, especially if moving them would create confusion.
Anything sensitive or messy enough that it needs cleanup before import should probably be held back until someone validates it. The main rule is to bring in what people need to work on immediately, not every historical artifact on day one.; [interview_turn:T072] I’d treat it as a tentative guideline for now, not a firm rule. If we make it too rigid too early, we’ll probably end up forcing bad imports or slowing the rollout. Better to keep it flexible and confirm the edge cases with the team once we’ve tested the process.
